title: Cloudflare Launches Kitesurf, a Browser Engine Built From Scratch for AI Agents
excerpt: The new engine uses 3–7× less compute than Chromium, trading pixel-perfect rendering for efficiency as the race to build AI-native browsers accelerates.
body:
• Cloudflare has launched Kitesurf, a browser engine built from scratch for AI agents, not based on Chromium
  • Kitesurf uses 3–7× less CPU and memory than Chromium for common agent tasks like screenshots and HTML extraction
  • Built entirely on Cloudflare Workers using Rust and WebAssembly, the browser passes 215,000+ web platform tests
  • Available free in beta through Browser Run, with plans to open-source the project once it matures

Cloudflare has released Kitesurf, a new browser engine designed exclusively for AI agents, marking the company's first foray into building its own web browser after years of internal debate.

Unlike traditional browsers built on Chromium — the open-source engine behind Chrome, Edge, and most modern browsers — Kitesurf strips away everything a human user needs and focuses on what matters to AI: token count, context windows, scalability, and cost.

A Browser That Thinks Like a Machine

The premise behind Kitesurf is straightforward. AI agents increasingly need to browse the web to complete tasks — filling out forms, extracting data, taking screenshots — but desktop browsers were never designed for machine actors. They carry overhead from tabs, extensions, themes, and pixel-perfect rendering that AI models do not need.

https://x.com/ekcheungAI/status/2090725691805298915

"We should be giving all agents a browser that excels at what's important for an AI model, even if that means being light on what's only useful for humans."

— Cloudflare Engineering Blog

Cloudflare said it built Kitesurf in just 12 weeks, drawing initial inspiration from Obscura, an open-source Rust-based headless engine. The team used AI agents to accelerate development, with Web Platform Tests (WPT) providing clear goalposts for conformance.

The browser runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers, the company's serverless computing platform, using Rust compiled to WebAssembly. It incorporates components from Blitz's rendering engine, Firefox's Stylo CSS parser, and the Boa JavaScript engine for handling eval operations.

Performance: Less Compute, More Sessions

In Cloudflare's benchmarks across a 14-URL test corpus, Kitesurf delivered substantial resource savings compared to Chromium.

For screenshots, Kitesurf used 380 milliseconds of CPU versus Chromium's 1,173 milliseconds — 3.1 times less. Memory usage was even more dramatic: 57.8 MiB for Kitesurf versus 271 MiB for Chromium, a 4.7× reduction.

HTML extraction showed similar gains, with Kitesurf consuming 3.8 times less CPU and 7 times less memory than Chromium. The trade-off is wall-clock speed — Kitesurf takes 1.7 to 1.8 times longer to complete tasks because it lacks Chromium's JIT compiler optimizations.

"Less memory means we can run more sessions, scale better, and fundamentally lower both our costs and yours," the company said.

Where Kitesurf Falls Short

Cloudflare is upfront about what Kitesurf cannot do. It does not yet support video playback, WebGL rendering, or TLS fingerprint negotiation for bypassing bot challenges. Long-running authenticated sessions requiring persistent state still need Chromium.

The browser correctly renders common pages including TodoMVC variants, Wikipedia, Hacker News, and parts of the Cloudflare dashboard, but complex web applications may hit compatibility gaps. Cloudflare is adding hundreds of passing WPT tests weekly.

The Broader Race for AI Browsers

Kitesurf enters a space that is drawing significant attention. OpenAI expressed interest in acquiring Google Chrome in April 2025 if antitrust regulators forced a sale, signaling the strategic value of browser technology for AI development. Other projects like Lightpanda are also targeting lightweight browsers for automation.

Cloudflare's advantage is integration with its existing infrastructure. Kitesurf works with Puppeteer, Playwright, and any AI agent that speaks Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), meaning developers can switch to it without retooling. It also supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) used by AI coding tools.

What's Next

Kitesurf is available for free during its beta period through Browser Run, with per-account usage limits. The company plans to open-source the project once it is ready, letting customers deploy their own instances.

Development priorities include expanding CDP coverage, improving rendering fidelity for screenshots and PDFs, and continuing to close the WPT gap. The team is also working on reducing the wall-time penalty compared to Chromium.

For developers building AI agents that need web access at scale, Kitesurf offers a cost-effective alternative — as long as they can accept the trade-offs of a browser that is still very much in its early days.
